transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Alex Morales (BrightForge CTO), Samir Patel (BrightForge Infra Lead), Riley Chen (BrightForge PM)

Summary:
BrightForge is evaluating Redwood's hosted API for a quick PLG onramp but has heavy privacy and compliance constraints that might push them toward Dedicated or Private deployment. They want time-to-first-token <= 3 days for a prototype, SOC2 evidence, and a performance benchmark plan. Next steps include security docs, pilot pricing, free credits, and a deeper infra benchmark session.

Topics:
- Quickstart / free credits / PLG path
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (VPC, KMS, on-prem)
- Performance: batching, KV cache, quantization, latency vs cost
- Pilot scope, success criteria, stakeholders

Action items (from call): see metadata field 'action_items'

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:14] Alex (BrightForge): Hey Jordan, doing good thanks. Quick note, recording's fine. We've got a tight window to get a PoC going.
[00:22] Priya (Redwood SE): Hi all, yeah, excited to dig in. We'll run through hosting options, a fast path with free credits, and then benchmark ideas.
[00:31] Samir (BrightForge): Cool. To start, our constraints: data classification is PII-ish, some redacted customer info, and our security team is, well, strict. We need SOC2 evidence, SSO, and KMS integration for keys.
[00:45] Riley (BrightForge PM): Also timeline: product org wants a prototype in two weeks ideally. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is a metric we're tracking.
[00:55] Jordan: Understood. For TTFT, our PLG hosted path typically gets teams to first token within hours, most often under a day if they use our SDK and quickstart. But I know with security reviews that can stretch — we'll send the free credits so you can start immediately against sandbox endpoints.
[01:12] Alex: When you say sandbox endpoints, is that still hosted by Redwood or a customer VPC? Our risk team asks about data never leaving our control.
[01:24] Priya: Good question. Sandbox is on hosted infra with tenant isolation; data is ephemeral and not persisted to training. If your security team insists on customer-controlled keys or network egress restrictions, Dedicated or Private (VPC or on-prem) are the paths. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and isolated tenancy; Private gives you a customer VPC and can be on-prem. Both support KMS/HSM integrations.
[01:50] Samir: Right, the KMS bit is critical. Can you integrate with AWS KMS or do you force Redwood KMS?
[01:58] Priya: We support bring-your-own-key (BYOK) for Dedicated and Private deployments via AWS KMS and partner HSMs. Hosted customers use Redwood-managed encryption by default, but we can negotiate a managed HSM for enterprise with contractual controls.
[02:15] Alex: And audit logs/auditing? Our compliance requires tamper-evident logs.
[02:21] Jordan: We provide audit logs, per-request tracing, and longer retention as an add-on. For Private deployments, logs can be routed to your SIEM. We'll include sample audit-log formats in the security pack.
[02:33] Riley: For the prototype, what would you recommend — start hosted with obfuscated payloads, or go straight to a VPC pilot?
[02:42] Priya: Typical pattern: start hosted to validate product flows and UX — that gives the fastest TTFT — then move to Dedicated once you have volume and need isolation, or to Private if compliance requires network controls.
[02:55] Alex: Cost concern: we have a naive model dev budget. Dedicated sounds expensive. Any ballpark?
[03:03] Jordan: We'll send a pilot pricing sheet. For small pilots we often propose a temporary reserved pool (lower capacity) plus usage-based overage. It's cheaper than full production reserved upfront. We'll put numbers in the follow-up.
[03:18] Samir: On performance, we have two workloads: short chat-like queries (avg seq 128) and document summarization (avg seq 1,024). Latency sensitivity varies. Can Redwood support both without manual rewriting of code?
[03:33] Priya: Yes, our runtime supports model variants and auto-routing. We can route short, latency-sensitive traffic to a lower-latency model or to a dedicated low-latency pool, and heavier summarization to a batch-optimized path. Also, features like KV cache and prefix caching help for chat scenarios.
[03:51] Alex: Can you explain KV cache in non-magical terms?
[03:54] Priya: Sure — KV cache stores key/value pairs for transformer state between tokens; for chat it avoids recomputing earlier tokens, dropping per-token compute and latency. It's especially helpful for long histories. It's automatic in our SDK when you enable caching.
[04:10] Riley: Does caching create data residency issues? Where's the cache stored?
[04:14] Priya: By default it's in-memory on the serving nodes; for Dedicated/Private we can constrain it to your VPC and control retention.
[04:22] Samir: Good. About quantization for cost savings — do you do automatic quantization or do we need to re-compile models?
[04:30] Priya: We have quantized model variants and a recommendation engine in Redwood Optimize. For pilots, we can recommend a quantized variant that's drop-in compatible for inference. Some model-specific tuning helps; we'll include suggested quantization profiles in the benchmark plan.
[04:44] Alex: Is there any loss in quality we can expect? Our product is quality-sensitive.
[04:49] Priya: Small quality tradeoffs at aggressive quant levels. Part of our Optimize flow is to run evals against your prompts to measure regression and recommend acceptable quant levels.
[05:00] Jordan: To prioritize, we'd like to scope a two-week pilot: Day 0 — account + credits + basic quickstart, Day 1-3 — integrate SDK and hit first token, Day 4-10 — run benchmark suite, Day 11-14 — review and decide Dedicated vs Private / production plan.
[05:18] Alex: First token in 1-3 days is fine. But our compliance team will need the SOC2 report. Can you send it?
[05:25] Jordan: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 Type II and our network diagram in the security pack.
[05:32] Samir: One more networking nuance: egress / IP allowlists. We need to know the IPs for hosted endpoints and whether we can peer via PrivateLink.
[05:42] Priya: Hosted endpoints use regional egress ranges; we can provide the CIDR list. For PrivateLink or VPC peering, that's part of the Private/Dedicated setup. We'll include the standard network options in the security doc.
[05:53] Riley: Who's the technical contact for the benchmark session?
[05:56] Alex: Samir on infra plus Riley for product flows.
[06:00] Priya: Great, Samir, I'll own the benchmark plan and we can run two scripts: latency p95 for chat, and throughput for summarization (tokens/sec). We'll also test cold KV cache vs warm cache.
[06:12] Samir: Sounds good. We'll provide representative request traces and model sizes.
[06:17] Jordan: Are there any blockers from a legal/procurement perspective?
[06:20] Alex: Procurement wants to understand renewal terms if we move to Dedicated — and they want an SLA. Does Redwood offer SLAs for Dedicated?
[06:28] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. We'll outline the SLA tiers in the follow-up.
[06:36] Riley: On auth, SAML SSO + RBAC is required for our product team access.
[06:41] Priya: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls on both Hosted (enterprise tenant) and Dedicated/Private.
[06:50] Samir: Ok, practical question: if we start on Hosted for TTFT and then migrate to Dedicated, is there a big migration effort?
[06:57] Priya: We build migration paths — you can pin model versions and use the same API surface. For KV cache and state, there are considerations, but generally it's a config and routing cutover rather than code rewrite. We'll document migration steps.
[07:10] Alex: Do you support on-prem as an air-gapped option? Our legal folks asked.
[07:15] Jordan: Yes, Private includes on-prem packaging for regulated customers, though that's a longer engagement with additional integration work.
[07:23] Riley: For the pilot, what metrics do we need to prove to product leadership?
[07:27] Jordan: TTFT, p95 latency for chat (target <150ms for short prompts if you use low-latency model), cost per 1k tokens, and quality regression metrics versus a baseline eval set.
[07:39] Samir: 150ms p95 seems optimistic for 128 tokens. Can you achieve that on standard GPU infra?
[07:45] Priya: It depends on model size and region. For smaller, optimized models we can hit that with continuous batching disabled (single-request low-latency pool) and specialized kernels. For larger models, p95 will be higher. We'll include model-specific expected latencies in the benchmark doc.
[08:00] Alex: Any examples of customers with similar constraints?
[08:04] Jordan: Yes — a payments company (we anonymize customer names) moved from hosted to dedicated due to PCI-like constraints and used our Dedicated pool with BYOK. Priya can share an anonymized case study.
[08:15] Priya: I'll put together a case summary and a short graph of latency vs cost for a couple of model families.
[08:22] Riley: About SDKs: we prefer a Node.js and Python SDK. Are both supported?
[08:26] Jordan: Yes, official SDKs for Node/Python/Go; plus a simple REST path.
[08:31] Samir: For load testing, do you provide any benchmark harness or should we run our own?
[08:36] Priya: We provide a benchmark harness and sample scripts; for the pilot we'll customize it to your traces.
[08:43] Alex: Let's talk credentials and access. How do we onboard engineers without creating security noise?
[08:49] Priya: We'll create scoped API keys with per-key RBAC and expiry. For hosted quickstart, keys can be created in the console and scoped tightly. For Dedicated/Private, keys can be provisioned via SSO grants.
[09:00] Samir: On the free credits — what's the process to accept them? We want to ensure they go to a controlled account, not ad-hoc.
[09:06] Jordan: We'll provision a trial org for BrightForge and assign credits. Admin access can be controlled via SSO or invite links.
[09:13] Riley: Can we have two sandboxes: one for product and one for infra tests?
[09:17] Priya: Yes, we can create separate projects under the org and allocate credits per project.
[09:23] Alex: If we find we need private network connectivity mid-pilot, how fast can that be stood up?
[09:29] Priya: PrivateLink or VPC peering for Dedicated often takes 2-3 weeks due to networking approvals; Private on-prem is longer. But we can bridge with a hybrid config for low-risk testing.
[09:41] Samir: For model onboarding — we plan to use an open LLM fine-tuned internally. Can we bring our own model artifacts?
[09:49] Priya: For Private deployments you can host your own model artifacts. For Hosted and Dedicated, we support bringing model weights in some cases via sealed transfer, but there's an onboarding security review. We'll discuss specifics in the tech deep dive.
[10:00] Riley: Who will review the legal terms?
[10:02] Alex: Our legal team will take the standard agreement then mark up. They'll want data residency and indemnity language clarified.
[10:09] Jordan: We'll loop in legal and send a draft with pilot terms.
[10:13] Alex: Okay — hands-on questions: how does Redwood handle fallbacks when capacity is constrained? We can't have user-facing errors.
[10:21] Priya: We have smart routing and automatic fallback to compatible model variants and regions. You can configure an automatic degrade policy to a lower-capacity but faster model or a synchronous queued response. That helps keep services available with graceful degradation.
[10:36] Samir: Interesting. On metrics collection — can we export traces to Datadog?
[10:40] Priya: Yes, we have integrations with Datadog and other observability platforms; traces and per-request token usage can be exported.
[10:46] Riley: For cost control, any quick levers?
[10:49] Jordan: Batching configuration, quantized model variants, and route-level quotas. Our console has token-level cost breakdown and alerts.
[10:58] Alex: Let's capture success criteria for pilot.
[11:01] Jordan: Pilot success criteria: 1) Integration within 3 days and first token; 2) p95 latency within agreed targets for chat; 3) Quality regression <= X% (we'll agree on metric); 4) No unacceptable compliance blockers discovered.
[11:15] Samir: Agree. For the quality metric we prefer an F1-like score on our eval set but we can define it in the benchmark doc.
[11:24] Priya: We'll include an eval harness and help run the first pass.
[11:29] Jordan: OK, logistics: I'll send the security pack and pilot pricing after the call. Priya will own the technical benchmark plan and set up the PLG org and credits.
[11:40] Riley: Can you also include a short runbook for migrating from Hosted to Dedicated? Our SREs would like that.
[11:45] Priya: Yes, migration runbook included.
[11:48] Alex: One last question on data retention: if we use hosted sandbox, what's retention policy?
[11:54] Jordan: By default, no retention for hosted quickstart. For production hosted customers we have configurable retention windows; we'll include the default in the security doc.
[12:04] Samir: Good. Any blockers from the Redwood side for starting the pilot immediately?
[12:08] Jordan: No blockers. We'll provision credits and a trial org after today's call.
[12:12] Riley: Great. Let's schedule the tech deep dive early next week — Tuesday?
[12:15] Priya: Tuesday works for us. We'll send calendar options.
[12:19] Alex: Thanks everyone.
[12:21] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and invites.
[12:26] (silence / wrap)

End of recording.

Notes about transcript quality and errors: occasional mis-attribution of speaker names, some transcription artifacts (e.g., 'BYOK' recognized correctly most times, but 'private link' sometimes transcribed as 'privateplink'), and some technical terms may be shorthand.
